title: Japanese verb tenses
summary: Japanese has two tenses, non-past and past. "Is doing" is a white engine, て + いる, and time words follow a simple に rule.

blocks.text: So far every verb has been in its plain dictionary form. Japanese has just **two tenses**: the **non-past** (the dictionary form) and the **past**. There is no separate present and no separate future. This lesson has four parts: the non-past, the past, the **ている** form for "is doing", and time words.
1. The non-past is not a present tense
Think of the non-past like English "I eat at six": it covers habits, facts, and above all **things that will happen**. So 犬が食べる most naturally means "The dog will eat."

blocks.en: The dog will eat. (or: The dog eats.)

blocks.text: The past says that something has already happened. It is made by changing the end of the verb, and the result is called the **た-form**. For verbs like 食べる and 見る it is simple: **drop る and add た** (食べる → 食べた). Most other verbs change their last kana in a few fixed ways: 飲む → 飲んだ, 行く → 行った. Lesson 5 gives the full recipe. The **て-form** is the same as the past with **て** instead of **た** (食べた → 食べて); the next section uses it.

For something happening **right now**, Japanese uses **いる** together with the **て-form** of the verb. 食べて is a **white engine**: a verb that cannot pull the train alone but adds information to the real engine, いる. The core of the sentence is 犬がいる, "the dog is"; 食べて tells us what the dog is doing. In this ている pattern, いる works for anything that is doing something, even rain: 雨が降っている.
犬が食べている。 The core is 犬がいる; 食べて says what the dog is doing.

A **relative** time word (relative to now: 明日 tomorrow, 今日 today, 昨日 yesterday) goes at the start of the sentence with **no particle**. An **absolute** time (a day of the week, a clock time) takes **に**. A good rule of thumb: if English would say "on / at / in", Japanese uses に.

blocks.jp: 明日（私が）ケーキを食べる。
火曜日に（私が）ケーキを食べる。

blocks.text: 明日（私が）ケーキを食べる。 明日 has no に; 火曜日 needs に.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Two tenses only: **non-past** (dictionary form) and **past** (**た**: 食べる → 食べた, 飲む → 飲んだ).
The non-past usually points to the **future** or to a habit.
**て + いる** says an action is **in progress**.
Relative time (明日, 今日): **no particle**. Absolute time (火曜日, 六時): **に**.
